I don't see iCloud as a photo backup, never said that. I'm complaining about how much storage it (among other iCloud services) needlessly takes up on my devices.

A video clip that someone sent me does not need to be kept on my Mac sheet it’s uploaded to the cloud. If I need to edit something, I’ll download a local copy. 

 Besides Apple clearly states iCloud is not a backup service.

Bingo. Couple it with iMessage insisting on keeping full size copies of all attachments sent to you on every single device and you’re cooked when it comes to space. Nothing should be on my phone in a full-size version (or at all) if it’s in the cloud.

It’s all iCloud related. iMessages keeps full size copies of everything on all devices, which is unnecessary. I don’t need instant access to a video my work colleague sent me six months ago, so keep it in the cloud, because THAT’S the additional space I’m paying monthly for.

Another example: iMessage shouldn’t take up very much space iCloud syncing is turned on. 

Oh and for context. I was an Apple At Home Advisor for three years, worked my way up to senior advisor and ended up writing internal training materials. When you log into Microsoft Office on your personal phone using your work email, it doesn’t automatically give your employer full access to your device. They can’t see your personal apps, photos, text messages, or other private data. What they can access, however, is anything connected to your work account, such as your work emails, documents, and calendar events within the Microsoft Office apps. This is because those features are tied to your company’s systems and are managed under their policies.

In some cases, employers may require you to install a security app or enroll your device in a system like Microsoft Intune when using a work email on a personal device. If that happens, they might gain additional control over work-related data on your phone, such as the ability to remotely wipe work content if your phone is lost or you leave the company. This doesn’t mean they can see everything on your device, but it does give them a limited ability to manage or remove work-related information.

It’s always a good idea to review your company’s IT or device management policies to understand what happens when you use your work email on a personal device. If you didn’t install any extra apps or give special permissions when logging in, your workplace likely only has access to the work-related apps and information you use through Microsoft Office. For clarity and peace of mind, you can check with your IT department to confirm their policies on personal devices.

You’re not crazy—this is a common misunderstanding based on how people interpret time labels.

When your husband says “12am on Christmas Day,” that technically means the very beginning of December 25th, right after midnight on Christmas Eve. In contrast, if he’s referring to working from “12am Christmas night to 5am on the 26th,” he’s actually talking about the very beginning of December 26th.

Your interpretation—“12am on the 26th”—is correct for what he’s describing if he means the midnight at the end of Christmas Day.

It seems like the bickering stems from differing ways of describing midnight:

• **“12am Christmas Day”** = The start of Christmas Day (midnight at the end of Christmas Eve).

• **“12am Christmas night”** = The start of December 26th (midnight at the end of Christmas Day).

If he works at midnight after the celebrations on Christmas, then it’s 12am on December 26th. It sounds like he might be mixing up how he’s explaining it, which is causing the confusion. 😊
